title: Taylor's Inequality
short: Bound the error of a Taylor polynomial.

blocks.html: A Taylor polynomial is an approximation. How good is it? Taylor's inequality bounds the error using the next derivative, much as the Mean Value Theorem bounds how far a function can move.

Write $f(x) = T_n(x) + R_n(x)$. Taylor's theorem says the remainder has the form
$$R_n(x) = \frac{f^{(n+1)}(c)}{(n + 1)!}(x - a)^{n+1}$$
for some $c$ between $a$ and $x$: it looks just like the next term of the series, with the derivative taken at an unknown point. (For $n = 0$ this is the Mean Value Theorem.) You do not know $c$, but if you know a bound $M$ for $|f^{(n+1)}|$ on the whole interval, you get a guaranteed error bound.

Taylor's inequality: if $|f^{(n+1)}(t)| \le M$ for all $t$ between $a$ and $x$, then $$|\role[error after degree n]{remainder}{R_n(x)}| \le \frac{\role[bound on the next derivative]{constant}{M}}{(n + 1)!}|\role[distance from the center a]{input}{x - a}|^{n+1}.$$ If $R_n(x) \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$, the Taylor series converges to $f(x)$.

blocks.title: A sine estimate
blocks.q: Bound the error when $T_3(x) = x - \frac{x^{3}}{6}$ approximates $\sin(0.5)$.
steps: Every derivative of $\sin$ is $\pm\sin$ or $\pm\cos$, so $M = 1$ works.
(Actually $T_3(0.5) = 0.479167$ and $\sin 0.5 = 0.479426$: the true error is $0.00026$, well inside the bound.)

blocks.title: How many terms for e?
blocks.q: How many terms of $e = \sum\frac{1}{n!}$ guarantee an error less than $0.001$?
steps: For $f(x) = e^{x}$ on $[0, 1]$, every derivative is at most $e < 3$, so $M = 3$.

blocks.name: taylor
blocks.cap: Taylor polynomials of $e^{x}$ with a probe at $x = 1$. The readout shows the actual error; compare it with the bound $\frac{3}{(n + 1)!}$ as you raise $n$.

blocks.html: Choosing $M$ from the value at the center only. For $e^{x}$ on $[0, 2]$, $f^{(n+1)}(0) = 1$, but the bound must hold for every $t$ in the interval, and $e^{t}$ reaches $e^{2} \approx 7.39$. Using $M = 1$ would understate the error. Find the largest value of $|f^{(n+1)}|$ on the whole interval between $a$ and $x$ (or a convenient number above it).

blocks.title: Why the series for e^x works
steps: On the interval between 0 and $x$, $|f^{(n+1)}| \le e^{|x|}$, so $|R_n(x)| \le e^{|x|}\frac{|x|^{n+1}}{(n + 1)!}$.
So $R_n(x) \to 0$, and the series converges to $e^{x}$.
